name: Glycopyrronium tosylate (Qbrexza)

lead: Qbrexza is a once-daily prescription cloth that cuts heavy underarm sweating, so users keep clothes free of sweat marks and feel more at ease in social settings.

It blocks the muscarinic receptors that signal sweat glands to produce sweat, with limited absorption into the bloodstream. The FDA approved it in June 2018 for ages 9 and up, and Japan approved it in 2022. Two randomised 4-week phase 3 trials, ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2, found it reduced sweating more than vehicle, and a 44-week open-label study followed.

paras: It is wiped across clean, dry underarms once a day. People typically notice drier underarms within the first weeks of use.
Dry mouth and local skin reactions are described, and case reports describe pupil dilation from transfer to the eye. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Qbrexza is a once-daily underarm wipe that cuts heavy underarm sweating, so users keep clothes free of sweat marks and feel more at ease in social settings. It blocks the signal to the sweat glands. It is FDA-approved for axillary hyperhidrosis and supported by phase 3 trials.

lead: Glycopyrronium tosylate is a topical anticholinergic applied as a once-daily cloth to the underarms for primary axillary hyperhidrosis, or excessive underarm sweating. Its appearance payoff is dry underarms: fewer visible sweat patches and stained clothing, which is the problem people with hyperhidrosis most often describe. Sold in the US as Qbrexza (2.4 percent cloth), it was approved by the FDA in June 2018 for people aged 9 and older and in Japan in January 2022 [1][2].

Its approval rests on two replicate phase 3 trials, ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2, which compared 3.75 percent glycopyrronium tosylate (the salt strength corresponding to the 2.4 percent glycopyrronium cloth) with vehicle for 4 weeks and found it reduced sweating severity and production versus vehicle [3][4]. A 44-week open-label extension and pediatric analyses followed [5][6]. A 2019 review describes it as a self-administered, non-invasive alternative to topical antiperspirant therapy and clinic-based treatments [7].

Its use outside hyperhidrosis clinics is mostly by people who want sweat control for social, professional or athletic reasons; a lifting forum thread, for instance, mentions the wipes while discussing slippery palms and grip [8]. The drug is prescription-only [1].

paras: Hyperhidrosis is sweating beyond what the body needs for temperature control. A 2019 review says it affects over 4.8 percent of the US population and that severe primary hyperhidrosis can interfere with daily activities and quality of life [9]. Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article reports that over 80 percent of patients describe moderate to severe emotional effects, and that people may avoid handshakes, struggle to grip objects or change shirts repeatedly [2]. It describes a treatment ladder that begins with high-strength aluminium chloride antiperspirants, and continues with iontophoresis for hands and feet, botulinum toxin injections for the underarms, oral anticholinergics and surgical options [2].

It blocks muscarinic receptors on eccrine sweat glands, reducing the activation of the glands by acetylcholine [9]. A pharmacokinetic study compared the cloth with oral glycopyrrolate: systemic absorption was lower with the cloth, with no accumulation over repeated use and similar exposure in adults and children, and no anticholinergic adverse events occurred in the phase 1 cloth group while dry mouth and nasal dryness occurred with the oral drug. The authors noted that this depends on following the instructions: wipe each underarm once with the same cloth, wash hands and avoid contact with the eyes [10]. In population analyses, the frequency and severity of anticholinergic events rose with higher glycopyrronium concentrations, with no link between blood levels and efficacy [10].

Across the 44-week extension, 8.0 percent of 550 analysed patients discontinued because of adverse events. The commonest events were dry mouth (16.9 percent), blurred vision (6.7 percent), application-site pain (6.4 percent), nasopharyngitis (5.8 percent) and mydriasis (5.3 percent), and most patients had no local skin reaction [5]. In the Japanese study, the commonest events were photophobia, mydriasis, thirst and dysuria, mostly mild [11].

Pupil dilation from accidental eye contact is the best-characterised issue. A multicenter case series of 16 patients with pharmacologic mydriasis found that half were 18 or younger, 87.5 percent had one enlarged pupil, none who reported hand hygiene details had washed their hands after application, and 37.5 percent wore soft contact lenses; the authors concluded it reflects local exposure rather than systemic toxicity and that patients often do not mention the cloth as a medication [12]. Case reports describe a 2-month-old infant with unilateral mydriasis after parental use of the wipes, and a young woman with blurred vision, dry mouth, absent sweating and urinary hesitancy after overuse [13][14]. Reviews describe anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and local skin reactions [15].

ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2 were randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled 4-week phase 3 trials. Patients were randomised 2:1 to 3.75 percent glycopyrronium tosylate or vehicle once daily in each underarm. In pooled data, 59.5 percent of treated patients versus 27.6 percent on vehicle reached the responder threshold on the sweating-severity item of a patient diary, and gravimetric sweat production fell by 107.6 mg per 5 minutes versus 92.1 mg per 5 minutes with vehicle at week 4. Authors listed the short duration and the difficulty of weighing sweat as limitations [3].

Patient-reported outcomes from 463 treated and 234 vehicle patients showed greater improvement with the drug at every week: by week 4 the severity, impact and bothersomeness diary scores improved by 62.6 versus 34.0 percent, 65.5 versus 40.3 percent and 65.4 versus 39.0 percent, with similar advantages on quality-of-life measures [4]. In the pediatric subgroup (ages 9 to 16, 44 patients), improvements were comparable to older patients [6].

In the 44-week open-label extension, 564 of 651 completers continued, and at week 44 the share reaching a 2-grade improvement on the Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale was 63.2 percent, with sweat production down 71.3 percent from baseline; no new safety signals emerged [5]. A Japanese randomised study of 497 patients (3.75 percent, 2.5 percent, vehicle) reported responder rates of 51.6, 41.1 and 16.4 percent at week 4 [11]. Registered trials have also explored palmar hyperhidrosis (an open-label phase 2 study with 120 participants) [16], and a withdrawn registration planned to compare a 1 percent glycopyrronium cream with the cloth under maximum use [17].

Qbrexza was approved in the US in 2018 and in Japan in 2022, where Maruho launched it [1]. A 2024 Medical Letter review covers sofpironium, a related topical anticholinergic approved for the same condition [18]. A T Nation thread mentions the wipes in a discussion about summer grip [8].

timeline.event: FDA approval of Qbrexza for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in people aged 9 and over [1].
